requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'DFlash: Block Diffusion for Flash Speculative Decoding' have been reproduced.

The AdamW optimizer with cosine LR schedule and warmup is available and correctly wired up in the training loop configuration (learning rate 6e-4, gradient clipping 1.0, warmup ratio 0.04, 6 epochs).

The DFlash draft model architecture (block diffusion drafter with shared embedding/LM head, bidirectional attention, and configurable layer count/block size) has been implemented as described in Section 4.1.

The overall draft model module exists with configurable depth, block size, and hidden dimension matching the target model, and integrates the sub-components (embedding, LM head, transformer layers, KV injection).

Code has been implemented that defines a DFlash draft model class parameterized by number of layers, block size, hidden size, and number of target hidden features, so that the same class can instantiate the various DFlash configurations used in the paper (e.g., 3/5/8-layer, block size 8/10/16).

Code has been implemented that constructs the default DFlash draft model with 5 transformer layers for Qwen3-4B/8B and block size 16, and with 8 layers for Qwen3-Coder (block size 16) and 10 for LLaMA-3.1 draft models, matching Section 5 implementation details.

Code has been implemented so that instantiating the draft model exposes standard forward-pass interfaces (input token ids + injected target features -> output logits over the vocabulary) usable by both training and speculative decoding inference paths.
The draft model shares the token embedding layer and language modeling head with the frozen target model, with only the draft transformer layers being trainable.
Code has been implemented that binds the draft model's input token embedding to the target model's embedding tensor (shared parameters, not a copy), so both point to the same weight matrix.
Code has been implemented that ties the draft model's LM head to the target model's LM head (shared weights), so draft logits are produced in the target model's output space.

Code has been implemented that freezes the shared embedding and LM head parameters (requires_grad=False) and freezes all target-model parameters during draft-model training, leaving only the draft transformer layers (and the target-feature projection) trainable.
A unit-style behavioral check verifies that a training step updates only the draft transformer layers (and target-feature projection) while embedding/LM head/target parameters remain unchanged.
Each draft transformer layer uses bidirectional (non-causal) self-attention within a block combined with the appropriate cross-block masking, matching Figure 2/Figure 4.

Code has been implemented that constructs a draft-layer self-attention with bidirectional attention among tokens within the same draft block (mask tokens and any anchor/clean tokens attend to one another without causal masking).
Code has been implemented such that draft tokens attend to the injected target-context KV entries for their own positions/history, providing conditioning at every layer.

A behavioral test verifies that a masked token at position k inside a draft block receives non-zero attention weight to other positions inside the same block (both earlier and later positions), confirming bidirectionality within a block.

The draft model applies per-layer KV injection of a shared, MLP-fused target context feature into every draft transformer layer's Key and Value projections, as described in Section 4.1 and Section A.3.

Code has been implemented that maintains a single shared projection matrix W_c of shape (D, 5D) (or (D, num_features*D) in general) that maps concatenated target hidden states to the draft hidden dimension, and this projection is used across all draft layers.

Code has been implemented so that at each draft layer i, the projected target context features are passed through the layer's Key and Value projections (W_K^i, W_V^i) to produce additional KV entries, while draft tokens produce their own Q/K/V normally.

Code has been implemented such that the injected target features bypass the draft-layer Q projection, output projection, self-attention state update, and FFN, i.e. they only appear as additional K/V entries for masked draft tokens to attend to.
Code has been implemented that stores the per-layer injected K and V tensors in the draft model's KV cache so they can be reused across drafting iterations without recomputation.

A behavioral test confirms that when the same input and target features are provided but KV injection is disabled, the draft model's output logits change materially, and that with KV injection enabled the layers actually consume the projected target features (e.g., zeroing the injected KV changes outputs).
The draft model supports block-diffusion drafting: given a clean anchor/context token, it predicts the next block_size - 1 masked positions in parallel in a single forward pass.
Code has been implemented that defines a mask token id (or reserved embedding) used to fill the block_size - 1 positions to be predicted in parallel by the draft model.

Code has been implemented that produces draft logits for all block_size - 1 masked positions in a single forward pass conditioned on a preceding clean anchor token and the injected target context features.
A behavioral test verifies that the draft model, given block_size = 16, returns a logit tensor of shape (..., 15, vocab_size) for the masked positions in a single forward call.
The draft-model configuration is flexible enough to reproduce the specific per-model settings reported in the paper (layer counts, block sizes, number of target hidden features).
Code has been implemented that supports 3, 5, and 8 draft-layer configurations (as used in the layer-count ablation in Table 6) with block size 16 and 5 target hidden features.
Code has been implemented that supports block sizes 8, 10, and 16, matching the block-size ablation (Table 8) and the LLaMA-3.1 (block size 10) / Qwen3 (block size 16) production settings.

Code has been implemented that supports selecting either 3 or 5 uniformly-sampled target hidden features to concatenate before projection, matching the ablation in Table 7 and the default 5-feature setting.
The draft model's parameter and memory footprint match the paper's claims about being a lightweight adapter.

For the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B configuration (draft hidden size D = 2048, 5 target features, BF16), the shared target-feature projection W_c has size approximately 5 * 2048 * 2048 parameters and consumes about 42 MB of parameter memory, as claimed in Section A.3.

The extraction of hidden features from uniformly sampled target model layers, the projection/fusion through the shared Wc matrix, and the KV injection mechanism into every draft layer have been implemented correctly.
Hidden features are extracted from a fixed set of target model layers uniformly sampled from shallow to deep during target-model forward passes.

Code has been implemented to hook or otherwise capture hidden states from a configurable set of intermediate transformer layers of the frozen target model during its forward pass (both prefill and verification).
The number of extracted target hidden features defaults to 5, and the sampled layers are uniformly spaced between the second layer and the third-to-last layer of the target model.
The number of extracted layers is a configurable hyperparameter (supporting at least 3 and 5 features) to enable the ablation on the number of target hidden features.

Code has been implemented for both online extraction (compute target hidden states on the fly during training) and offline extraction (precompute and cache target hidden states, then load them during draft training).
The extracted hidden states are concatenated across sampled layers and projected through a single shared linear layer Wc to produce a compact fused target context feature.
Code has been implemented that concatenates hidden features from the N selected target layers along the hidden dimension prior to projection.

A single shared projection matrix Wc of shape (D, N*D), where D is the draft hidden dimension and N is the number of extracted target features, projects the concatenated hidden states to the draft hidden dimension exactly once (not per layer).
The projected fused target context feature is shared by all draft layers (i.e., the projection output is computed once per token and reused across every draft layer's KV injection).
For a Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-scale configuration with D=2048, N=5, and BF16 weights, the Wc parameter memory footprint is approximately 42 MB (matching the paper's reported overhead).
The fused target context feature is injected as additional Key and Value entries into every draft model layer, bypassing draft-side Q, output projection, self-attention update, and FFN.
Code has been implemented so that at every draft layer i, the fused target context feature is projected through per-layer K and V projections (W_K^{c,i}, W_V^{c,i}) to produce additional KV entries.
The target-derived KV entries are concatenated with the draft tokens' own K and V entries and attended to by the draft tokens' queries within self-attention.
The target context feature is NOT projected through the draft model's Q projection, output projection, self-attention update, or FFN — it only enters as additional K/V entries.
The KV entries derived from target context features are stored in the draft model's KV cache and reused across drafting iterations without recomputation.
KV injection is applied to every draft transformer layer (not only the input layer), providing consistent conditioning throughout the draft model depth.
The attention masking of target context features integrates correctly with draft-side bidirectional block attention during both training and inference.
Draft tokens within a masked block attend bidirectionally to their corresponding injected target context feature KV entries, matching the design shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4.
During inference block-diffusion drafting, all masked positions within a block share access to the same set of target-context KV entries in a single forward pass.

Measured behavior confirming that KV injection substantially outperforms input fusion for target-feature conditioning under both autoregressive and block-diffusion drafting on Qwen3-4B with 5-layer draft models and block size 8.
Under block-diffusion drafting with KV injection (DFlash), acceptance length on GSM8K reaches approximately 4.2 and speedup reaches approximately 3.3x over baseline (Table 9).
Under block-diffusion drafting, switching from input fusion to KV injection consistently increases acceptance length on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MT-Bench (matching the KV > Input pattern in Table 9).

Under autoregressive drafting, DFlash-AR (5-layer with KV injection) achieves higher acceptance length than EAGLE-3-5L (input fusion) on GSM8K (~4.8 vs ~4.2), HumanEval (~4.6 vs ~4.3), and MT-Bench (~3.4 vs ~3.1).

The DFlash training pipeline — including random anchor sampling of masked blocks, sparse Flex Attention masking across concatenated blocks, exponentially decaying position-weighted cross-entropy loss, frozen embedding/LM head, and AdamW/cosine schedule hyperparameters — has been implemented.
Training data preparation: responses regenerated by the target model and used as the training targets for constructing the DFlash draft training set.

Code has been implemented that constructs the training set by generating responses with the target model from prompts drawn from the mixture of NVIDIA Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2 and CodeAlpaca (approximately 800K samples), rather than using the original dataset responses.

Code has been implemented that formats each training example as a concatenation of clean prompt tokens and clean target-model response tokens with a maximum sequence length of 3072 tokens (4096 tokens for Qwen3-Coder).
Random anchor sampling of masked blocks tailored to the speculative decoding setting.
Code has been implemented that randomly samples 512 anchor positions per training sequence, using each anchor as the first (clean) position of a masked block.
Code has been implemented so that within each sampled block the anchor token is kept clean while the remaining (block_size - 1) positions are replaced with mask tokens for parallel prediction.

Code has been implemented that re-samples the anchor positions for every sequence at every epoch, so the number of masked blocks per sequence stays fixed while positions vary across epochs (data-augmentation strategy for efficient long-context training).

Under an ablation using 100K training samples with a 3-layer draft model, block size 16, and 5 target hidden features, the random anchor sampling strategy yields higher acceptance length and speedup than a standard block-diffusion sampling baseline on Math500, HumanEval, and MT-Bench (matching Table 13).
Sparse Flex Attention masking over concatenated blocks that enforces intra-block bidirectional attention and disallows cross-block leakage.
Code has been implemented that concatenates all sampled masked blocks from a sequence into a single joint sequence processed in one forward/backward pass.

The sparse training attention mask allows tokens to attend bidirectionally to other tokens within the same block and to the corresponding injected target context features, while attention across different blocks is disallowed.

Code has been implemented that constructs this sparse attention pattern using Flex Attention (Dong et al., 2024) so multiple draft blocks are trained efficiently in a single forward and backward pass.

The attention mask preserves causal consistency with the prompt/response so that masked positions within a block can see the block's clean anchor(s) and the corresponding target-context KV entries but cannot see clean or masked tokens from other blocks.
Exponentially decaying position-weighted cross-entropy training loss that emphasizes earlier positions within each draft block.
Code has been implemented that computes per-token cross-entropy loss only at masked positions inside each block, using the target model's next-token distribution / ground-truth token as the target.

Code has been implemented that applies an exponentially decaying weight to the cross-entropy loss for a token at position k within a block, with earlier positions weighted more heavily than later ones.
The loss-decay hyperparameter gamma is configurable and defaults to 7 for block size 16, 5 for block size 10, and 4 for block size 8.

In an ablation on Math500, the version trained with exponential loss decay converges faster and reaches a higher acceptance length than the uniform-weighting variant across training epochs (matching Figure 5).
Frozen shared embedding and LM head with only the draft transformer layers being trained.
Code has been implemented that shares the token embedding layer and the language modeling head between the draft model and the target model.
The shared embedding layer and LM head have requires_grad disabled and are excluded from the optimizer's parameter list so their weights remain frozen throughout training.
Only the draft transformer layers (and associated projections such as the target-feature fusion projection and per-layer KV injection projections) are included in the trainable parameter set.
AdamW optimizer with cosine learning-rate schedule and specified training hyperparameters.
Code has been implemented that uses the AdamW optimizer to update the trainable draft-model parameters.
The training script uses a peak learning rate of 6e-4, a cosine schedule with warmup ratio 0.04, and gradient clipping with max-norm 1.0.
The draft models are trained for 6 epochs over the data mixture.
Online and offline training modes for target hidden feature computation.
Code has been implemented supporting an online training mode in which target hidden features are computed on the fly from the frozen target model during each training step.
Code has been implemented supporting an offline training mode in which target hidden features are precomputed and cached, then loaded during draft-model optimization to reduce compute overhead.

In both modes, the entire clean prompt+response sequence is passed through the target model once per example to extract hidden features from the uniformly sampled layers, then these features are fused (via the shared projection W_c) into the draft hidden dimension before being injected as KV entries during draft-model training.

sub_tasks.requirements: The end-to-end speculative decoding inference loop with target-model verification, bonus token handling, and both greedy and temperature-sampled acceptance criteria has been implemented for DFlash and baselines.

The overall speculative decoding cycle structure (prefill -> draft -> parallel verify -> accept/reject -> bonus token -> next cycle) is implemented as a top-level loop that can be invoked with any (target_model, draft_model) pair.

Code has been implemented that performs an initial prefill pass on the target model over the input prompt, produces the first sampled token, and initializes the target model's KV cache before entering the speculative decoding loop.

Code has been implemented for a main decoding loop that repeatedly calls the drafter to propose gamma draft tokens, invokes the target model to verify them in parallel, applies the acceptance rule, appends accepted tokens plus the bonus token to the running output, and terminates on max-token or EOS conditions.

Code has been implemented that, on each cycle, uses the last clean token produced by the target model (the bonus/verified token from the previous verification step) as the anchor conditioning the next draft block, matching the DFlash inference-time contract described in Section 4.1.
Parallel verification of the draft block by the target model, including position/attention setup and logits extraction for each candidate position, is implemented.

Code has been implemented that feeds the gamma draft tokens (plus context) into the target model in a single forward pass with correct position ids and causal attention, producing target logits at each of the gamma+1 candidate positions in one call.

Code has been implemented that correctly manages and rolls back the target model KV cache after verification so that only accepted tokens (and the bonus token) persist in the cache for the next cycle.

Greedy (temperature = 0) acceptance criterion is implemented: for each draft position, the draft token is accepted iff it equals the target model's argmax; acceptance stops at the first mismatch and the target argmax becomes the bonus token.

Temperature-sampled acceptance (Leviathan-style rejection sampling with temperature = 1) is implemented: for each draft position, acceptance probability min(1, p_target(x)/p_draft(x)) is applied, on rejection a token is resampled from the residual distribution max(0, p_target - p_draft) normalized, and on full acceptance a bonus token is sampled from p_target.

Code has been implemented that always appends one bonus token from the target model per verification cycle (whether all drafts were accepted or the first rejection triggered a resample), so the effective accepted-per-cycle count lies in [1, gamma+1] as required by the tau definition in Section 3.1.

The verification loop supports DFlash's block-diffusion drafter: it accepts a full block of gamma tokens produced by a single parallel draft forward pass, verifies them left-to-right against the target model, and honors the block size (e.g. 16 for Qwen3, 10 for LLaMA-3.1, 8 for ablations).

The verification loop supports the EAGLE-3 baseline drafter, including tree-structured drafts with configurable draft-tree size (e.g. 10, 16, or 60), draft steps = 7, and top-k = 10, and applies tree-attention verification against the target model.

Code has been implemented that measures and returns the average acceptance length tau per cycle (total accepted tokens including bonus divided by number of verification cycles) so it can be reported per benchmark as in Tables 1, 2, 3, and 5.

Code has been implemented that measures end-to-end wall-clock decoding speedup of speculative decoding over vanilla autoregressive decoding from the same target model with matched generation settings (max 2048 new tokens, same prompt, same temperature).

The implementation produces lossless output under greedy decoding: sequences generated by the DFlash speculative loop with temperature = 0 are token-identical to sequences generated by pure autoregressive decoding of the same target model on the same prompts.

The implementation preserves the target model's sampling distribution under temperature = 1: the empirical token distribution from the speculative loop is statistically indistinguishable (within tolerance) from that of vanilla temperature-1 sampling from the target model on matched prompts.

The measured average acceptance length tau for DFlash with block size 16 on Qwen3-8B at temperature = 0 matches the paper's reported average (approximately 6.49 across the 7 benchmarks in Table 1) within reasonable tolerance.

The measured end-to-end speedup of DFlash over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-8B at temperature = 0 averages approximately 4.86x across the 7 benchmarks in Table 1, matching the paper's headline result within reasonable tolerance.

Both the autoregressive decoding baseline and the EAGLE-3 speculative decoding baseline (with tree sizes 16 and 60, top-k=10, 7 draft steps, using AngelSlim Qwen3 checkpoints and the official LLaMA-3.1 EAGLE-3 checkpoint) have been reproduced faithfully for comparison against DFlash.
The autoregressive (vanilla) decoding baseline used for computing DFlash/EAGLE-3 speedups has been implemented and integrated with each evaluation backend.

Code has been implemented to run standard autoregressive decoding of the target LLM (LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B/8B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, and additional models) with a maximum generation length of 2048 tokens for the main experiments.

Code has been implemented to run the autoregressive baseline under both greedy decoding (temperature=0) and stochastic sampling (temperature=1) configurations, matching the experimental settings used in Tables 1 and 2.

Code has been implemented to support the autoregressive baseline on all three evaluation backends used in the paper: HuggingFace Transformers (for Tables 1, 2), SGLang with FA4 / Flashinfer (for Tables 3, 5), and vLLM (for Table 12).

Code has been implemented to measure per-token latency (L_target) and end-to-end throughput of the autoregressive baseline, providing the denominator for speedup computation (η = L_target / L_DFlash) across all benchmarks.

The autoregressive baseline on Qwen3-8B (Transformers backend, temperature=0) produces speedup=1.00× on GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME25, HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, and MT-Bench, serving as the reference used in Figure 1 and Table 1.
The EAGLE-3 speculative decoding baseline has been reproduced with the specified drafting configuration (top-k=10, 7 draft steps, tree sizes 16 and 60) and the correct pretrained draft checkpoints.

Code has been implemented to run EAGLE-3 speculative decoding as the comparison baseline, including the autoregressive draft model, tree-based draft expansion, and parallel verification by the target model.
EAGLE-3 is configured with 7 draft steps and top-k=10 per step for all reported experiments (Table 1, Table 2, Table 5).

EAGLE-3 supports two tree-size settings: tree size 16 (matching DFlash block size 16 for equal drafting budget) and tree size 60 (as used in the original EAGLE-3 paper to maximize acceptance length), both selectable at inference time.
The Qwen3 EAGLE-3 draft checkpoints used for baseline comparison are loaded from AngelSlim (Tencent) rather than being trained from scratch, matching the paper's Section 5 statement.
The LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct EAGLE-3 draft checkpoint used in Section 5.5.1 is the official checkpoint released by the EAGLE-3 team (trained on UltraChat and ShareGPT).

Code has been implemented to compute EAGLE-3's average acceptance length τ (average number of accepted tokens per verification cycle, including the bonus token) as reported alongside speedup in Tables 1, 2, and 5.
The reproduced EAGLE-3 baseline achieves the numerical speedups and acceptance lengths reported in the paper on Qwen3-4B/8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B benchmarks.

EAGLE-3 with tree size 16 on Qwen3-8B (Transformers backend, temperature=0) achieves an average speedup of approximately 1.76× and average acceptance length τ ≈ 2.96 across GSM8K/MATH-500/AIME25/HumanEval/MBPP/LCB/MT-Bench, matching Table 1.
EAGLE-3 with tree size 60 on Qwen3-8B (Transformers backend, temperature=0) achieves an average speedup of approximately 2.02× and average acceptance length τ ≈ 3.40, matching Table 1.
EAGLE-3 with tree size 16 on Qwen3-4B (Transformers backend, temperature=0) achieves an average speedup of approximately 1.81× and average acceptance length τ ≈ 3.05, matching Table 1.
EAGLE-3 with tree size 60 on Qwen3-4B (Transformers backend, temperature=0) achieves an average speedup of approximately 2.08× and average acceptance length τ ≈ 3.48, matching Table 1.
EAGLE-3 with tree size 16 on Qwen3-4B/8B under temperature=1 sampling achieves average speedups of approximately 1.72× and 1.68× respectively across the seven Table 1 benchmarks.

EAGLE-3 with 10 draft tokens on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (SGLang Flashinfer backend, Spec-v1, single B200) achieves an average acceptance length τ ≈ 3.49 on GSM8K, ≈ 3.62 on HumanEval, and ≈ 3.11 on Alpaca, matching Table 5.

EAGLE-3 with 60 draft tokens on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (SGLang Flashinfer, single B200) achieves acceptance lengths τ ≈ 4.55 on GSM8K, ≈ 4.65 on HumanEval, and ≈ 4.07 on Alpaca (Table 5), with speedups that degrade below 1× at concurrency 32.

The main comparison experiments on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with thinking mode disabled (Table 1) across GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME25, HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, and MT-Bench at temperature 0 and 1 have been reproduced, matching reported speedups and acceptance lengths.
The evaluation harness runs Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B non-thinking generation with all seven benchmarks and reports both speedup and average acceptance length metrics.
Evaluation Setup and Configuration
Code has been implemented to run the Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B-Instruct target models with thinking mode disabled (e.g., enable_thinking=False in the chat template) for the Table 1 experiments.
Code has been implemented to cap generation at a maximum of 2048 tokens per request for all benchmarks in Table 1.
Code has been implemented to run all Table 1 experiments using the Hugging Face Transformers backend (not SGLang/vLLM) on NVIDIA H200 GPUs.
Code has been implemented that supports evaluation at both temperature = 0 (greedy) and temperature = 1 (stochastic sampling) sampling modes for the same models and benchmarks.
Code has been implemented to configure DFlash drafting with block size 16 for all Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B non-thinking Table 1 runs.

Code has been implemented to configure EAGLE-3 baselines with tree size 16 (matching DFlash block-16 drafting budget) and tree size 60 (as used in the EAGLE-3 paper), with draft steps = 7 and top-k = 10 in both cases.

EAGLE-3 draft latency scales approximately linearly with the number of draft tokens across {4, 8, 16}, consistent with sequential autoregressive drafting cost T_draft ≈ γ · t_step.

DFlash draft latency increases monotonically with draft-model depth (1 < 3 < 5 layers) at each fixed draft-token count in the measured curves.
